NEW YORK/LONDON, Oct 23 : Stock indexes were mixed on Friday, with tech shares edging higher after the previous day's selloff, while Brent crude oil rose to its highest in more than five months after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia. The Nasdaq was up 0.2 per cent after starting the day lower, while the Dow was last down about 1 per cent. An index of semiconductors was up about 1 per cent. It posted its biggest daily percentage drop since June on Thursday after a report from Meta Platforms reignited worries about the AI trade. It's been "a very volatile week," said Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B. Riley Wealth in Boston.

"After Meta's report, there's still anxiety over the AI trade to a certain extent," he said. "But also, we continue to be in a place where things look like they're getting worse, not better, in the Middle East. That moves energy prices higher, which is obviously going to end up being a significant headwind for economic activity." Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia fanned fears over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East, where United Arab Emirates authorities also reported an oil spill. US crude rose 2.56 per cent to $102.02 a barrel and Brent climbed to $116.27 per barrel, up 2.74 per cent. European natural gas prices jumped.  AMEX, TELECOM SHARES FALL Investors were digesting corporate earnings news. American Express shares fell 3.5 per cent after it reported results and its CEO said the company had good momentum, but needed to become a more "agile and efficient" organization. Telecom company shares, including Verizon, dropped after a Bloomberg News report that SpaceX was in talks with cellular infrastructure companies about launching a US wireless carrier program. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 476.25 points, or 0.9 per cent, to 52,391.73, the S&P 500 eased 11.14 points, or 0.14 per cent, to 7,652.96 and the Nasdaq Composite rose 52.51 points, or 0.21 per cent, to 26,062.75. MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe fell 1.64 points, or 0.15 per cent, to 1,121.29.The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 0.4 per cent. Asia's bourses steadied overnight, with South Korea's KOSPI ending its session higher after shedding as much as 4 per cent earlier. US Treasury yields rose a day after the benchmark 10-year yield registered its biggest one-day drop in nearly four years, but remained under 5 per cent. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note was last up 3.7 basis points at 4.992 per cent. The 10-year yield is down about 11 basis points on the week and on pace for a third straight week of declines, its longest run lower since June. EURO FALLS The euro fell and was on track for a weekly loss against both the US dollar and the yen, while euro zone bonds stabilized after recent volatility. Investors' focus has been on concerns over France's finances. French yields, which were down 5 basis points at 5.04 per cent, have risen nearly 27 bps this week, the most of any major euro zone country and the most in a week since late May.  A selloff in French government bonds this week pushed the country's debt risk premium to its highest level since the euro zone sovereign debt crisis in 2011. France will deploy 70,000 police backed by specialist units for protests on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said. The country faces the threat of a rating downgrade by Moody’s later on Friday. The euro was last down 0.12 per cent at $1.12, set to end the week 0.35 per cent lower.

Oct 23 : US telecom stocks declined on Friday after a report that SpaceX was seeking thousands of cell sites for a fourth wireless carrier, fueling concerns over fresh competition. Elon Musk's rocket and space technology company was in talks to access at least 80,000 cell sites to build its wireless carrier from scratch, Bloomberg News reported late on Thursday, citing sources familiar with the matter. AT&T fell 5.6 per cent to a more than three-month low, Verizon lost 1.6 per cent and T-Mobile shed 5 per cent.  Germany's Deutsche Telekom, which holds an over 50 per cent stake in T-Mobile, lost 3.2 per cent.

"The competitive impact may still be years away, but anticipation alone, reinforced by each successive spectrum and infrastructure move, is likely to remain an overhang on sector sentiment," Bernstein analysts said in a note. The report comes weeks after SpaceX acquired low-band spectrum to advance its carrier plans, mounting a direct, orbital challenge to legacy wireless giants in the US and sending AT&T and Verizon shares to their worst one-day falls in more than two decades. Bernstein analysts said that an MVNO (mobile virtual network operator) deal with SpaceX may not appeal to telecom operators, but a unified stance against one has done little to lift sentiment, leaving carriers to reassess their options. SpaceX's Starlink has been generating revenue from internet services in sparsely populated and rural areas, but becoming a true rival to major carriers will require years of work and a terrestrial network. Tower operator Crown Castle, however, surged 11.6 per cent after the report identified it as one of the cellular infrastructure companies SpaceX was in talks with.  Other operators also rose, with American Tower up 4.9 per cent and SBA Communications adding 4.6 per cent.  Shares of SpaceX rose 1.7 per cent.

Oct 23 : Telecom giants AT&T and T-Mobile are investing to safeguard customer data and network infrastructure from new cybersecurity threats as AI integration ramps up, though fully autonomous networks remain years away, company executives told Reuters. As AI agents automate workflows and data analysis, with declining human intervention, cybersecurity concerns are growing across industries over access to sensitive information and connected software. For telecom operators, which manage vast amounts of customer data and critical communications infrastructure, vulnerabilities in AI systems or third-party software could extend from data breaches to network disruptions. "Yes, we are increasing our investments in how we monitor and react," T-Mobile's Chief Technology Officer John Saw told the Reuters Global Markets Forum. The company simultaneously works with vendors to ensure security holes are closed as soon as possible, he added.

The Bellevue, Washington-based wireless carrier has suffered several data breaches, including incidents in 2021 and 2023, cumulatively impacting over 100 million customer accounts. It has agreed to various settlements with consumers and the Federal Communications Commission involving cybersecurity penalties and investments. AT&T, meanwhile, warned that third-party software providers and AI agents pose cybersecurity risks that extend beyond operators' own networks. "There (are) industry problems, not things that AT&T can solve by itself," CTO Jeremy Legg said, questioning if the open-source community followed comparable security standards. The Texas-based company has deployed AI governance controls such as encryption, multi-factor authentication and human oversight of data access. It is also working to verify whether third-party AI agents seeking access to customer accounts are acting on behalf of legitimate customers, the company said. AI has automated aspects of network management for telecom operators, but handing over entire networks to AI-driven autonomous systems is still "years away," Legg said, as human intervention is still required to solve complex network problems. For instance, AT&T has automated some tasks such as analyzing trouble tickets to identify potential fixes and, in some cases, automatically implementing repairs. T-Mobile, meanwhile, uses AI to automatically adjust cell-site antennas when nearby sites go down to compensate for coverage gaps. During Winter Storm Fern in January, T-Mobile's self-organizing network, or SON, restored coverage to about 66 per cent of customers within an hour and 90 per cent within eight hours, with most customers regaining service before power was restored, Saw said. "While such warnings do not indicate a security breach, they can affect the normal operation of a website," Magwenya said. He added that the website was taken down as a precaution. PHP underpins a large share of the public web and is widely used by content management systems including WordPress, Drupal and Joomla, giving any critical vulnerability potentially widespread consequences. PHP developers on Wednesday released fixes for the flaws and urged users to update affected systems immediately.

WASHINGTON, Oct 23 : Six more companies, including Wells Fargo, Arm Holdings and Intuit, will not allow their shares to be tokenized on a joint trading platform backed by crypto exchange OKX and Intercontinental Exchange, according to a regulatory document seen by Reuters.  The new objections, which have not been previously reported, underscore the growing challenges for tokenization, the creation of digital tokens that represent a stock and can be traded on a blockchain similar to cryptocurrencies, despite the US securities regulator recently approving the novel products.  In total, 22 companies have objected, according to the document, which outlines the rules of the OKXICE venture and which companies have objected. It does not say why the companies objected. Sixteen of the companies, including Microsoft and Alphabet, are listed on Nasdaq. The others are listed on the New York Stock Exchange, which ICE owns. Nasdaq has teamed up with Payward, the parent of crypto exchange Kraken, to launch its own tokenized stock platform next year.

OKX and ICE had planned to tokenize 63 stocks through their joint venture, but have encountered objections from issuers. OKX and ICE filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission earlier this month to launch tokenized stocks under the agency's new innovation exemption. The exemption allows platforms that facilitate trading of tokenized stocks to operate without complying with many requirements that apply to traditional stock exchanges.  Under the exemption, platforms must notify companies before listing tokenized versions of their stocks, and cannot proceed if the issuer objects.   Speaking to reporters this week, Andrew Cuomo, co-chairman of the OKXICE joint venture, said given how revolutionary tokenization could be, it was natural for companies to take a "wait and see" approach, CoinDesk reported. While Nasdaq says it welcomes tokenization in principle, it has said such products should be subject to the existing set of rules and investor protections. It has warned that if improperly regulated, tokenization could fragment liquidity and undermine price discovery, among other issues.  "Given the risks we believe issuers must be cautious about their participation," the company warned in a September FAQ.  A Nasdaq spokesperson pointed Reuters to its FAQ. Although many overseas tokenized stocks are marketed like stocks, they rarely offer the same rights, disclosures and protections as traditional equities.  Under the SEC's exemption, tokenized stocks must confer the same rights and privileges as traditional securities, including the ability to receive dividends and exercise voting rights.

Oct 22 : Meta Platforms said on Wednesday that it is creating a new class of non-voting shares to fund its AI ambitions, pursue acquisitions and reward employees without weakening CEO Mark Zuckerberg's control. The move follows a structure used by some other founder-led companies, most notably Google's parent Alphabet. WHAT IS META DOING? Meta plans to create a new class of publicly traded non-voting stock, known as Class C shares, and distribute one Class C share for each existing Class A and Class B share — effectively splitting its stock two-for-one. The new shares are expected to begin trading in January 2027.

The company said in a filing that the Class C stock will be available for raising capital, compensating employees, acquisitions and other corporate purposes. Meta expects to offer new shares from time to time. WHY NOW? The investment required to compete in artificial intelligence is "unprecedented," Meta said. It has forecast 2026 capital expenditures of $135 billion to $145 billion, as it races to build data centers, buy chips and expand computing infrastructure for AI. Debt financing on that scale can adversely affect credit ratings, making equity financing more attractive, the company noted. The management wants the Class C stock available as early as the end of 2026, Meta said in its filing. HOW DOES THIS HELP ZUCKERBERG? The structure allows Meta to raise equity capital without issuing additional voting stock. Zuckerberg controls the company through his super-voting Class B shares. By issuing non-voting Class C stock, Meta can sell shares to investors, use them for acquisitions or employees compensation, without significantly reducing his voting power. Preserving Zuckerberg's leadership was a key objective of the recapitalization, Meta's special committee said, adding that he would not support a significant equity financing that reduced his voting control. The committee proposed sunset provisions on the dual-class structure, which would have converted his Class B shares into Class A on triggers such as his death or disability, his leaving the company or a major reduction in his equity. Zuckerberg, however, indicated he would not support sunset provisions or any move that would lead to losing voting control. "Meta has massive capital needs to fund its AI expansion," said Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at Stock Trader Network. "We've seen companies issue more debt to finance AI expansion and investors have punished those stocks for impairing their balance sheets," he added, pointing to the stock prices of Oracle and CoreWeave. "This is a better way to raise capital while keeping the balance sheet strong." HOW MANY SHARES WILL ZUCKERBERG RECEIVE? Like all existing shareholders, he will get one Class C share for each Class A and Class B share he owns. As of October 1, 2026, he beneficially owned about 341.2 million Class B shares and 1.2 million Class A shares — representing about 60.6 per cent of Meta's voting power and an ownership position of 13.4 per cent. So, he will receive about 342.4 million Class C shares. Only 20 per cent of the Class C shares received by the "Holder Group" — Zuckerberg and some of those to whom he is permitted to transfer his shares to — will be freely saleable immediately, according to a separate Founder Alignment Agreement. The remainder will be subject to restrictions designed to prevent him from monetizing his stake without a corresponding reduction in voting influence. WHO HAS DONE THIS BEFORE? Google is the closest precedent. It announced plans for a non-voting Class C stock dividend in April 2012, and a shareholder class action followed in Delaware. Google settled, and the court approved the deal in October 2013. Under the settlement, Google agreed to compensate Class C holders if the shares traded at a discount of more than 1 per cent to Class A over the first year. The Class C stock dividend was distributed on April 2, 2014, and in 2015, Google determined it owed Class C holders a $522 million adjustment payment based on the percentage discount between Class A and Class C share prices. WHY DOES ZUCKERBERG WANT THEM? One motivation discussed in the filing is California's Proposition 40, a proposed wealth tax on the November 2026 ballot. It would impose a one-time tax equal to 5 per cent of net worth on billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026. It taxes accumulated wealth rather than income. Meta said Zuckerberg told the special committee he was evaluating whether to relocate because of the potential multibillion-dollar tax liability. The Class C structure would allow him to sell some non-voting shares without immediately reducing his voting control. Meta's board said Zuckerberg's existing ownership stake sufficiently aligns his interests with shareholders and therefore does not warrant additional cash compensation or equity awards, a position it said it has maintained for years.

North American firms continue to steer spending toward AI, cloud services and US-based AI startups, weighing on traditional IT providers, Vasu said, adding the region could remain a laggard for the next two to four quarters. "Our Q2 has been softer and we are seeing pricing pressure on the back of competitive intensity and higher ask of passing (on) (AI-led) productivity, which are baked in our revised guidance," CFO Jayesh Sanghrajka said in a conference call. Hi-tech and retail clients in North America scaling down their projects weighed on the region's performance, he added. Revenue from North America, which contributes more than half of Infosys' sales, fell 1.5 per cent in the second quarter, its weakest performance in two years. Excluding currency movements, revenue was up 1.5 per cent. Net profit rose 6.2 per cent to 78.23 billion rupees, but missed analysts' expectation of 79.29 billion rupees. NEW YORK, Oct 23 : US stock investors face a pivotal week, with corporate earnings reports led by major AI players and a Federal Reserve meeting both posing critical tests for a suddenly shaky market rally. Weakness in technology shares left investors on edge about the state of the AI trade that has driven the US equity bull market that just marked its fourth anniversary. The AI pullback deepened on Thursday, with the Nasdaq Composite posting its biggest one-day drop since June. Investors were disappointed by quarterly reports from Meta and Lam Research. Meta is one of the hyperscalers spending massively to build out data centers, while Lam is a high-flying semiconductor company, one of a group that has been among the biggest AI stock winners. Three other hyperscalers - Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon - headline a packed week of quarterly results, including about one-third of S&P 500 companies. The Fed's interest rate policy meeting on Wednesday also could rattle markets.

"There are a lot of balls in the air," said Nick Giorgi, chief equity strategist at Alpine Macro.  "Next week, you have a lot more tech earnings, and right now the market is taking a discerning eye as it relates to all the spending that goes along with artificial intelligence," Giorgi said. "The market's just not giving the benefit of the doubt to companies that are spending a ton of money on building this all out, which to us is actually very healthy, but still does augur for some short-term pain." Investors also have their focus trained on the US midterm elections on November 3, with growing bets that the Democrats will wrest control of the US Congress away from President Donald Trump's Republican party. The series of market catalysts could ratchet up volatility over the next couple of weeks and challenge optimism that has helped lift the benchmark S&P 500 index up about 12 per cent in 2026. HYPERSCALERS ON THE HOT SEAT Robust US profit growth has underpinned the stock market's gains this year in the face of headwinds including spiking Treasury yields and rising energy costs stemming from the Middle East conflict. With more than 100 companies having posted results so far, third-quarter S&P 500 earnings are on pace to have climbed more than 32 per cent from a year ago, according to LSEG IBES data. Next week is the busiest of the reporting season. "I think earnings will determine whether this ... tech pullback is a buying opportunity, or is there a deeper correction ahead," said King Lip, chief strategist at BakerAvenue Wealth Management. "What we need is just another round of really strong earnings." Alphabet and Microsoft report on Wednesday. Amazon's results are due Thursday. Focus will be on the guidance the companies give on capital spending plans and whether they are seeing returns on the massive outlays. Capital spending from hyperscalers, expected to be around $800 billion this year, is boosting the bottom lines for a wide swath of companies involved in the AI buildout. But investors are wary of the sustainability of such spending amid mounting financing costs. "Earnings are critical to the overall confidence level of the AI trade and how much longer the spend will continue," said Kevin Mahn, president and chief investment officer at Hennion & Walsh Asset Management. FED EXPECTED TO PAUSE ON RATES, FOR NOW Quarterly reports next week from chip companies Intel and Sandisk also could influence the AI trade. Elsewhere, other high-profile companies set to report next week include drugmaker Eli Lilly, oil majors Exxon and Chevron and industrial equipment giant Caterpillar.  The prospect for more interest rate hikes also comes into focus with the Fed meeting. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, in an effort to control above-target inflation, but Fed fund futures late on Thursday suggested only a 5 per cent chance the Fed will hike again when it gives its policy statement on Wednesday, according to LSEG data.  One factor: Investors are dubious that the Fed will want to increase rates just a week before the midterm elections. However, markets are leaning toward a hike at the next meeting in December, with futures suggesting an 80 per cent probability of such a move then. Walter Todd, chief investment officer at Greenwood Capital, said he will be watching for any hints about the rate path at Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference following the decision.  "Does he say something to give an idea about December, because right now the expectation is there is going to be a hike?" Todd said.

WASHINGTON, Oct 23 : Private plaintiffs' lawyers stand to collect up to $1.27 billion from New Mexico if the state's $25 billion court win against Meta Platforms this week is upheld, according to a Reuters review of a contract with the state.  New Mexico hired Chicago-based law firm DiCello Levitt to represent it in the Meta case, which alleged the tech company duped its users about who had access to their personal data on its Facebook platform. The state's 2025 contract with DiCello Levitt, reviewed by Reuters after a records request, says the firm can ask the judge overseeing the case to award it 20 per cent of the first $50 million of any eventual recovery, 15 per cent of the next $50 million, 10 per cent of the next $150 million and 5 per cent of any amounts over $250 million.  New Mexico and other states have turned to private law firms in a growing number of cases against major technology companies to buttress their legal teams against deep-pocketed defendants. The outside lawyers typically don't charge by the hour but are entitled to a cut of any winnings.

In the Meta case, a jury sided with the state in September, and a judge on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25 billion. Meta denied wrongdoing and said it will appeal. Legal experts including Villanova University law professor Peter Ormerod told Reuters this week that the company has a strong basis for arguing that the judgment should be reduced.  If New Mexico ultimately recovers $25 billion from Meta, DiCello Levitt's fees could reach $1.27 billion under the law firm's contract. The amount would come out of the funds Meta pays to New Mexico.    UNCERTAINTY OVER FINAL PAYOUT To be sure, Meta could win its appeal or the judgment could be trimmed, and the court is not obligated to award the firm the maximum fees allowed under its contract. DiCello Levitt declined to comment about its fees. New Mexico's lead lawyer at the firm, Corban Rhodes, in a statement called the court's decision a "defining moment for consumer protection and privacy." Randi McGinn, a New Mexico lawyer who worked with the DiCello firm in representing the state, told Reuters her small Albuquerque firm is entitled to collect about 33 per cent of its fees. DiCello's contract allowed the firm to designate other lawyers as subcontractors. McGinn, who delivered the state's opening statement and closing argument, cautioned that a final outcome in the case could take several years. “People will say it’s a lot of money. But the truth is, we won’t see any of that money unless we win an appeal,” McGinn said.  Contingency fee awards over $1 billion are exceedingly rare, said Fordham University law professor Howard Erichson. While New Mexico's contract caps fees for DiCello Levitt near 5 per cent, "the sheer size of the recovery means it could result in a massive fee here, so I would expect the court to examine it carefully," Erichson said. The New Mexico attorney general's office and a Meta spokesperson did not immediately respond to requests for comment about the legal fees. STATES TURN TO PRIVATE FIRMS Some companies and business groups say that giving private lawyers a stake in state enforcement actions can put lawyers' financial interests in conflict with public policy concerns. Defenders of the practice counter that it helps level the playing field for states going up against companies that can afford armies of lawyers.  The rewards can be substantial. Norton Rose Fulbright is set to receive more than $156 million in legal fees for representing Texas in a consumer privacy case that Google settled for $1.375 billion. Law firms Keller Postman and McKool Smith billed Texas $142.6 million in a consumer privacy lawsuit against Meta that led to a $1.4 billion settlement in 2024. DiCello Levitt's contract mirrors one between New Mexico and Motley Rice for a separate lawsuit alleging Meta fostered social media addiction and other harms on its platforms. Meta denies the claims. Motley Rice could seek up to $67.1 million in that case if appeals courts uphold a pair of rulings totaling $942 million against Meta. Wednesday’s ruling came in a case New Mexico filed in 2021 against Meta after disclosures that British political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica obtained data from as many as 87 million Facebook users without their consent. The now-defunct Cambridge Analytica used the data for voter profiling and targeting.
